query: What are the main climate risks for Kenya's agricultural sector?
synthesis:
Kenya’s agricultural climate risk is dominated by the interaction of **rain-fed production, rising temperatures, and increasingly unreliable water availability**. The Kenya Climate Smart Agriculture Strategy estimates that approximately 98% of agricultural systems are rain-fed, while another source describes agriculture as principally rain-fed. Exposure is especially high in arid and semi-arid lands (ASALs), which different sources estimate at about 80%–85% of Kenya’s land area and where pastoral livestock systems are prevalent. [Kenya Climate Smart Agriculture Strategy 2017–2026](https://www.adaptation-undp.org/sites/default/files/resources/kenya_climate_smart_agriculture_strategy.pdf) [Climate Risk Profile: Kenya (2021)](https://climateknowledgeportal.worldbank.org/sites/default/files/country-profiles/15724-WB_Kenya%20Country%20Profile-WEB.pdf) [Climate variability and climate change and their impacts on Kenya's agricultural sector](https://cgspace.cgiar.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/c9cf0b41-8e3e-4b21-8535-fc9ac641a694/content)

The main risks are:

1. **Drought and rainfall variability.** Drought is the most immediate and damaging hazard for rain-fed crops, pasture, livestock, food security, and rural incomes. Moderate droughts occur on average every three to four years and major droughts approximately every decade; prolonged droughts have become more common since 2000. [Climate Risk Profile: Kenya (2021)](https://climateknowledgeportal.worldbank.org/sites/default/files/country-profiles/15724-WB_Kenya%20Country%20Profile-WEB.pdf) Rainfall is also highly variable across locations and seasons. Kenya’s agricultural calendar depends heavily on the March–June long rains and October–December short rains, so changes in the timing, amount, or duration of rainfall can disrupt planting, crop development, and harvesting. [Climate Risk Profile: Kenya (2021)](https://climateknowledgeportal.worldbank.org/sites/default/files/country-profiles/15724-WB_Kenya%20Country%20Profile-WEB.pdf) This risk is particularly severe for pastoralists, because drought reduces pasture and water, increases livestock mortality, and weakens herd reproduction. [Climate variability and climate change and their impacts on Kenya's agricultural sector](https://cgspace.cgiar.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/c9cf0b41-8e3e-4b21-8535-fc9ac641a694/content)

2. **Rising temperatures and heat stress.** Kenya’s annual mean temperature has increased by approximately 1.0°C since the 1960s, according to the World Bank profile. Higher temperatures reduce crop and livestock productivity, increase evapotranspiration, dry soils and pasture, raise livestock water requirements, and increase irrigation demand. [Climate Risk Profile: Kenya (2021)](https://climateknowledgeportal.worldbank.org/sites/default/files/country-profiles/15724-WB_Kenya%20Country%20Profile-WEB.pdf) Heat stress is expected to be particularly consequential in lowland and already water-stressed areas, although some highland locations could experience limited benefits where warming removes temperature constraints and farmers have sufficient inputs and services. [Climate variability and climate change and their impacts on Kenya's agricultural sector](https://cgspace.cgiar.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/c9cf0b41-8e3e-4b21-8535-fc9ac641a694/content)

3. **Heavy rainfall, flooding, and erosion.** More intense extreme rainfall can cause flooding, waterlogging, crop damage, soil erosion, nutrient loss, livestock losses, and damage to roads, farms, storage, irrigation, and other agricultural infrastructure. Flooding can also interrupt markets and food supply chains, and may follow drought, compounding its effects. [Climate Risk Profile: Kenya (2021)](https://climateknowledgeportal.worldbank.org/sites/default/files/country-profiles/15724-WB_Kenya%20Country%20Profile-WEB.pdf) [Climate variability and climate change and their impacts on Kenya's agricultural sector](https://cgspace.cgiar.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/c9cf0b41-8e3e-4b21-8535-fc9ac641a694/content)

4. **Water scarcity, soil-moisture loss, and land degradation.** Drought, warming-driven evaporation, rainfall variability, erosion, and unsustainable land and agricultural-water management reduce water available for crops, livestock, and competing users. These pressures can degrade soil fertility and pasture, increase production costs, and make agriculture less viable in parts of the ASALs. [Kenya Climate Smart Agriculture Strategy 2017–2026](https://www.adaptation-undp.org/sites/default/files/resources/kenya_climate_smart_agriculture_strategy.pdf) [A Global Review of the Impacts of Climate Change and Variability on Agricultural Productivity and Farmers' Adaptation Strategies](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12076006/)

5. **Pests and diseases linked to unusual weather.** Climate-related pest outbreaks can add biotic stress to drought, heat, and water stress. The Africa adaptation report links heavy precipitation in the Horn of Africa to desert-locust outbreaks affecting Kenya and neighboring countries, while a broader review identifies increasing pest infestations and plant diseases as risks to agricultural productivity. [State and Trends in Adaptation 2022: Climate Risks in Africa](https://gca.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/01/GCA_State-and-Trends-in-Adaptation-2022_Climate-Risks-in-Africa.pdf) [A Global Review of the Impacts of Climate Change and Variability on Agricultural Productivity and Farmers' Adaptation Strategies](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12076006/) The broader review is not Kenya-specific, so the available evidence for the scale of crop-disease risk in Kenya is limited.

These hazards translate into lower and less reliable crop yields, livestock losses, declining pasture, damage to productive assets, higher food prices, and worsening food insecurity and rural poverty. The risks are not simply a consequence of declining annual rainfall: projections show a wide range of possible annual precipitation changes, while the more consistent concern is greater variability, changing seasonality, drought, and heavy-rainfall extremes. [Climate Risk Profile: Kenya (2021)](https://climateknowledgeportal.worldbank.org/sites/default/files/country-profiles/15724-WB_Kenya%20Country%20Profile-WEB.pdf) The available sources did not contain a single definitive Kenya-wide estimate of future agricultural losses, and their projected rainfall and production outcomes vary substantially by model and scenario.
